title: Quantitative Rules for Parallel Calibration and Drift-Resilient Maintenance of Large-Scale Superconducting Quantum Processors
authors: Zhihao Wu, Kechengqi Zhu, Shichuan Xue, Xinfang Zhang, Zhaohua Yang, Zhida Zhang, Shun Hu, Cong Li, Dingdong Liu, Kangding Zhao, Peng Luo, Lingling Lao, Xiang Fu, Mingtang Deng, Junjie Wu, Kai Lu
abstract: As superconducting quantum processors scale toward hundreds of qubits, manual calibration becomes increasingly costly and difficult to sustain. Here we address two system-level factors governing automated calibration, namely, crosstalk induced by parallel operations and temporal drift of control parameters. On a 66-qubit superconducting processor, cross-entropy benchmarking shows that single-qubit calibration tolerates full-chip concurrency with minimal fidelity loss, whereas CZ calibration requires a minimum coupler-graph distance of four to avoid elevated control errors. Continuous monitoring of representative qubit and coupler parameters further yields quantitative refresh rules that assign refresh priority by error-budget consumption. These results turn two conventionally heuristic choices, the concurrency density of calibration tasks and the refresh priority of each control parameter, into measurable operating rules. Implemented within an automated calibration framework, the rules support a six-qubit Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger state with a zero-noise-extrapolated fidelity of 89.64%, distance-dependent logical-error suppression in a single-cycle repetition-code benchmark, and a reduction of the mean single-qubit error from 0.023 to 0.011 on a 337-qubit processor, providing an experimentally grounded reference for the automated calibration and maintenance of current and future large-scale superconducting quantum systems.
summary: This paper tackles the scaling bottleneck in superconducting quantum processors by quantifying the impact of parallel operations and parameter drift. It establishes measurable operating rules—such as minimum coupler separation for CZ gates and error-budget-driven refresh schedules—that automate calibration. These rules enable high-fidelity quantum operations on large-scale devices.
main_problem: The paper addresses the challenges of scaling superconducting quantum processors by developing quantitative rules to manage crosstalk from parallel operations and temporal drift of control parameters during automated calibration.
main_result: The derived rules allow for high-fidelity state preparation (e.g., 89.64% fidelity for a six-qubit GHZ state) and significantly reduce single-qubit error rates on large processors.
method: The authors used Cross-Entropy Benchmarking (XEB) to quantify gate fidelity under varying parallel densities and implemented continuous monitoring to derive error-budget-based refresh priorities.
model_or_system: The work is performed on superconducting quantum processors, specifically utilizing a 66-qubit device with a tunable-coupler architecture, which is tested up to 337 qubits.
key_observables: Zero-noise-extrapolated fidelity, single-qubit error rate ($\epsilon$), and the minimum required coupler-graph distance ($d_C$).
important_parameters: Concurrency density of calibration tasks and the refresh priority assigned to individual control parameters.
main_assumptions: The study assumes that calibration choices can be converted from heuristic guidelines into measurable, quantitative operating rules based on error budgets.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the full calibration workflow, comparing XEB Pauli error distributions under different parallel densities, and showing the time evolution of key control parameters exhibiting measurable drift.
paper_structure: The paper systematically analyzes system-level limitations (crosstalk and drift), develops quantitative metrics for these limitations, and concludes by implementing an automated framework based on these derived rules.
why_interesting: It provides concrete, experimentally grounded protocols for maintaining coherence and fidelity in large superconducting quantum systems, which is critical for scaling quantum computation beyond current proof-of-concept stages.
